title: Find the Student that Will Replace the Chalk
statement:
A class has `n` students numbered `0` to `n - 1`, and a box starts with `k` pieces of chalk. The teacher visits the students in order `0, 1, ..., n - 1` and then starts again from `0`, cycling forever. Student `i` needs `chalk[i]` pieces to solve a problem: if at least that many pieces are left, the student uses them up; if strictly fewer than `chalk[i]` pieces are left, that student must go and replace the chalk, and the process ends.

Return the index of the student who replaces the chalk.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating student by student can take up to `k = 10^9` steps. But every full round of the class uses exactly the total of `chalk`, so whole rounds can be skipped with `k % total`. What is left is less than one round, and the student who runs out is the first one whose running total of chalk exceeds that remainder. Running totals only increase, so a binary search over the prefix sums finds that student.

## Approach

1. Build `prefix[i]`, the chalk used by students `0` to `i` in one round; `prefix[n - 1]` is the round total.
2. Skip whole rounds: `remaining = k % prefix[n - 1]`.
3. Student `i` can still solve their problem exactly when `prefix[i] <= remaining`. Binary search with `left` and `right` for the first index where `prefix[mid] > remaining`.
4. That index, `left`, is the student who replaces the chalk. It always exists because `remaining < prefix[n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`chalk = [5, 1, 5]`, `k = 22`. The prefix sums are `[5, 6, 11]`, so one round uses 11 chalk and `remaining = 22 % 11 = 0`. The search starts with `left = 0, right = 2`: `mid = 1` and `6 > 0`, so `right = 1`; `mid = 0` and `5 > 0`, so `right = 0`. The answer is student `0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): building the prefix sums is linear; the binary search adds only O(log n).
- Space: O(n) for `prefix`.

## Pitfalls

- The round total can reach 10^10, which overflows a 32-bit integer; use a 64-bit type for prefix sums in Java or C.
- A student with exactly `chalk[i]` pieces left still solves the problem; only strictly fewer triggers the replacement, so search for `prefix[mid] > remaining`, not `>=`.
- When `k` is a multiple of the round total, `remaining` is 0 and student 0 replaces the chalk.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of students |
| `prefix` | `prefix[i]` is the chalk used by students `0` to `i` in one round |
| `remaining` | chalk left after all whole rounds are skipped |
| `left`, `right` | binary search bounds over student indices |
| `mid` | the student index being tested |

narration.3: prefix[i] will be the chalk used by students 0 to i in one round.
narration.4: The first running total is just student 0's need.
narration.5: Extend the running totals across the class.
narration.6: Each total adds this student's chalk to the previous total.
narration.8: Whole rounds use prefix[n - 1] chalk each, so skip them all with a remainder.
narration.10: The answer lies somewhere from student 0...
narration.12: Narrow the range until one student is left.
narration.13: Test the student in the middle.
narration.14: If the chalk up to mid exceeds what remains, someone at or before mid runs out.
narration.15: Keep mid as a candidate and search to its left.
narration.17: Otherwise students 0..mid all succeed, so look after mid.
narration.20: left is the first student who cannot be served: the one who replaces the chalk.
